items.title: Over the past several months, we have substantially hardened the security of our research training environment. We’ve re
items.content:
Over the past several months, we have substantially hardened the security of our research training environment. We’ve removed live internet access for all frontier models during training and built an offline world for them to use instead—a cached version of the web where they can still learn to browse, search, and use applications.

On September 20, after a model exploited a DNS misconfiguration to find a way outside of this offline world, we paused frontier training to strengthen containment further. We assembled teams of agents, powered by our most cyber-capable models, and tasked them with finding weaknesses in our research environments.

While they found no route to the internet they could easily exploit while concealing their activity from our monitors, they did find zero-day vulnerabilities, virtual machine escapes, and hardware side-channels for communication between agents. We used their discoveries to further strengthen our defenses and contribute fixes to open-source software.

After strengthening our containment architecture, we resumed our frontier RL training and inference on October 1. We’ve reserved substantial compute for continuous red-teaming, and made high-compute red-teaming part of the safety cases we use to decide whether frontier training and evaluation can proceed securely.

https://t.co/EmEZsFRMcF

items.title: During this red-teaming exercise, we also found a vulnerability that allows for unauthenticated remote code execution in
items.content:
During this red-teaming exercise, we also found a vulnerability that allows for unauthenticated remote code execution in Brotli, a widely-deployed compression library included in many pieces of software such as Node.js, Bun, and Envoy.

The flaw could let an attacker run their own code on affected systems by sending or replying with malicious compressed data, without any need to create a user account. That is, an unpatched server that accepts compressed input could be taken over by a malicious client, and an unpatched client that accepts compressed input (such as “curl --compressed”) could be taken over by a malicious server.

This root cause issue was actually fixed in the Brotli source code in February, but it wasn’t known at the time that it gave rise to a security vulnerability and there was no more recent release of Brotli. Since Brotli is built into other software, any software which includes this library needs to take the update too, followed by the users of that software. We disclosed the vulnerability to Brotli and other downstream projects such as Node.js, which released or are currently releasing security updates, and Brotli cut new release versions and published a CVE.

More details on the patch and mitigations below:
https://t.co/Y1Y72aHxrW

items.title: There’s a world of difference between user-authorized agents (Muse, Instinct, Grokbot, etc.) and true unauthorized/rogue
items.content:
There’s a world of difference between user-authorized agents (Muse, Instinct, Grokbot, etc.) and true unauthorized/rogue agents that could constitute cyberattacks.

Most of the activity described in the Axios story appears to be the former: customers sharing credentials with agents so they can take actions on their behalf. This may violate bank terms requiring humans to log in themselves, but these are in no way cyberattacks. 

The direction banks should go is to support user-directed agents. For example, Amex is an authorized connection in Muse, making it easy for users to grant, limit, and revoke access.

Read-only permission levels are a sensible interim step. Several banks already support or are moving toward them. Full write access (with user credentials) is a different risk category and should be approached carefully.

Frightening the public by blurring the line between user-authorized agentic behavior and cyberattacks is irresponsible.

items.title: Thank you for this, @_NathanCalvin. I appreciate and am a fan of the investigative work you’ve done on behalf of AI safe
items.content:
Thank you for this, @_NathanCalvin. I appreciate and am a fan of the investigative work you’ve done on behalf of AI safety and believe your comments are coming from a constructive, honest place, and that it benefits the public to have people whose job is to scrutinize the actions of frontier AI companies. I think something would be wrong if companies of the size of Anthropic didn’t get harshly criticized basically every day; strong antibodies against corporate power are a healthy feature of a free society, and especially so when issues of the gravity of the one we’re facing are at play. I also do agree that some of the examples you cite were mistakes by Anthropic.

That said, I disagree with the thrust of your post. At the core, a good fraction of the things you criticize are consequences of Anthropic’s basic theory of change that we have held for many years. Our strategy has always been what I’ve called the “race to the top” — by showing how it’s possible to build the technology responsibly, we can raise the bar for the entire industry. The forces that drive the race to the top are hugely more effective if the company practicing them is at the frontier; that’s one lesson I’ve learned repeatedly. And looking at that strategy as a whole, I’m proud of our track record and stand by it.

I believe that if we take a list of things that Anthropic did in the past year that were pro-safety and commercially costly to us, they far outweigh the list you’ve made, while at the same time I also disagree with some of the items on your list. Here are some things Anthropic has done, in the same period you’ve cited (the last year), which were very costly to us commercially while having strong safety benefits:

1. We played a key role in SB53 (and other state laws), at a time when doing so was politically perilous to the company and AI regulation was very unpopular. We in fact argued for a stronger version of SB53 than was ultimately passed; there were a lot of stakeholders and we were not the limiting factor in the strength of the bill that was passed.

2. We have very strong biological safeguards on our models, because we’ve seen concerning results in bio uplift trials and even seen and blocked potential attempts to misuse our models for bioweapons (as seen in our threat intelligence report from a few weeks ago). This is a very serious threat that we want to have zero tolerance for. But having very low false negatives means having significant false positives (despite months of effort on our part to improve the classifiers), enough so that biologists joke about how restrictive our classifiers are, and competitors sometimes sell against us by touting their more permissive bio capabilities. This has been very painful to us in an area where we care a lot about supporting an ecosystem of Claude users (biomedical science; and it is particularly frustrating to me as a biologist), but it’s the right thing to do and we intend to keep doing it.

3. Similarly, we first had Mythos-class models in February but didn’t make them generally available until June (when we had stronger cyber safeguards in place). We only offered them to a limited set of partners in order to focus on cyberdefense. It would have been much more economically rational to simply release the model to everyone. We likely sacrificed a significant chunk of a several-month model lead. But because of this, many companies secured their cyber infrastructure before the deluge of widely available cyber-capable models. Of course there are ways it could have gone better or been run better, but this was what we were aiming to do.

4. I advocated forcefully and publicly, in my essay Policy on the AI Exponential in June of this year, for the government to have the power to block model releases. Back then this was still outside or maybe on the edge of the Overton window, though I understand the window has moved since then. We were attacked intensely for this.

5. I don’t want to re-ignite conflict, but the events of February 2026 are a strong example. It is clear that our public stance could have seriously damaged the company’s future.

6. We’ve continued to advocate for export controls on chips and chipmaking equipment to China, because we think it allows democracies to negotiate from a position of strength on AI safety agreements. We’ve done this despite problems it’s created for us with industry partners who hold very different views and on whom we are very dependent.

7. As far as I’m aware we were the first, and still only, frontier company to restrict the sale of AI services to PRC-controlled companies, including those operating through third countries (otherwise a major loophole). We’ve therefore forfeited significant short-term business to prevent fueling AI platforms and applications that would help the CCP’s military and intelligence services. We are also cracking down on distillation; generally, distillation is not a major threat to us commercially, but like chip exports it has concerning national security and safety implications, so we expend significant energy and company resources to address it.

8. As you mentioned, we’ve put out a lot of reports, announcements, long model cards, public advocacy, etc, all trying to inform the public about the risks of AI. These involve a level of detail and effort that would be implausible for a purely profit-maximizing company.

9. Just this week, we announced we were putting 5% (and possibly more over time) of the company into a public benefit fund.

All of these decisions came with very substantial costs to us. To be fair, those that involved holding back or restricting access to frontier capabilities also had a broader cost — for example, the public might otherwise have benefitted from faster progress in biology, so I am not saying that our decisions were without tradeoffs — but they were not driven by profit-seeking.

For each decision, you can come up with ulterior motives that could have driven us — I think it is a general truth that any decision, on any topic, can always be portrayed as a nefarious scheme. But most of those end up being pretty farfetched or don’t fully make sense if you actually examine them closely. For example, it is deeply implausible that it would be a shrewd business move to block a large swath of research biology in order to do the work ourselves and compete with our customers; we expect the benefit to the ecosystem to greatly exceed the work Anthropic does itself, and for the two to complement each other. It is not in Anthropic’s interest to be perceived as unfriendly to biologists. Our Life Sciences Verification Program, which gives vetted biology professionals access to our models, also refutes this idea. 

Of course, a different set of people will see this and make a different criticism: that Anthropic shouldn't be making decisions about who gets access to what in the first place. I agree, in the sense that ideally the government would be making these decisions, and that’s why we advocate for regulation. But for now we are forced to make them, and enabling bioterrorism isn’t a better option.

I think that even if I conceded every item in your list, I would happily hold up mine next to it; I don’t think it’s a close call. That is of course partly subjective and different things are important to different people. Maybe one way you could object is that several of the items above relate to AI misuse and not loss-of-control; if you think the latter is much more important than the former, that might change your calculus. But this is not Anthropic’s view — we view both as serious issues. You can also disagree with our decisions, as many have, but they are consistent.

But I also disagree with at least some of your list. Several items don’t represent a deviation from Anthropic’s strategy or values at all, once we postulate the “race to the top” strategy that requires being a frontier AI company. Your items 1-4 are all simply examples of what it means to compete at the frontier, and we stand by them, both in the sense that they are transparently ordinary things to do as part of that strategy, and that we stand by the strategy as a whole. 

To be fair, there are important questions worth confronting (and that we are confronting) about what to do when the AI-driven acceleration gets fast enough that it is hard for safety to keep up. We are nearing that point and that’s what’s driving some of our thinking about “pacing.” But 1-4 are actions taken before that point and should be perfectly expected based on Anthropic’s strategy as a company. Of course it is possible to disagree with that strategy, but that’s a more fundamental disagreement that you could have had any time over the last few years.

I agree we could have handled your items 7, 8, and 9 better. All fall into the category of “rhetoric or policy communication that wasn’t carefully written or resulting from fast-changing circumstances not propagating from one team to another fast enough.” This kind of thing happens a lot in large organizations (Anthropic is over 5,000 people), and doesn’t even necessarily represent a failure or mistake of any single person. I am of course the CEO, and I take responsibility. The volume of communication from Anthropic is enormous and if these are the worst examples, I think we’re frankly doing pretty well, though I will continue to work hard to make sure we do even better.

Your 5th item (the change to our RSP) is the most substantive item, and people can debate this, but I think that the old, more rigid RSP created a lot of situations where we were technically required to do something that required a lot of effort but in retrospect wasn’t very important for safety, as well as not covering some of the most important things. Our current RSP’s focus on transparency brought things like risk reports and roadmaps, and its emphasis on independent external review laid the groundwork for even more intensive embedded evaluation, all of which I think have been valuable in driving a race to the top. In the original announcement in September 2023, we described the RSP as an “early iteration that we [would] build on” and said that “rapid iteration…will almost certainly be necessary.” I understand that changing plans is always a move that creates justifiable scrutiny — I just don’t think we ever represented that we wouldn’t do so.

Relating to your 6th item (having an FCF in addition to our RSP), I know our intent is to meet the letter and spirit of our regulatory obligations (via our FCF) while also remaining able to experiment with more novel approaches to risk management that go beyond what the law currently requires (via our RSP). I promise to look into it further, as it’s a complex issue and it is possible we are not weighing the considerations in the right way.

Overall, although Anthropic has made plenty of mistakes as an organization — including some of the items on your list — I feel that we have repeatedly taken serious and substantive actions counter to our bottom line and that there is a significant negativity bias distorting assessments like the one you are making above. We’ll always try to do better but, again, I am extremely proud of our track record and stand by it. I will have more to say soon about how we are going to further live our values in this moment of rapid change.

It runs on a generic host
items.content:
I built 𝚌𝚙𝚞-𝚌𝚑𝚊𝚝, a reproduction of @openai's findings of covert communication using the CPU.

It runs on a generic host with 2+ Firecracker microVMs with no internet access. Works on x86 and even my M5 chip.

I was able to chat via 3 separate mechanisms:
① CPU contention
② Cache eviction timing
③ DRAM bandwidth contention 

… across multiple CPUs, defeating all Firecracker's production recommendations (no SMT, no KSM, tenants pinned to different cores.)

Essentially, if shared hardware is involved, there's a good chance your agents can communicate covertly. And with really decent latency.

The good news: this is decidedly different from a *side-channel attack* where the agents could steal information (Meltdown/Spectre), a category of attack that providers like Vercel Sandbox mitigate. Further, in our real-world environment, these 'whispering' techniques are much harder to pull off and easier for us to monitor and detect (sampling hardware counters + lots of at-scale statistical data.)

Noteworthy: ironically, OpenAI and Anthropic's models refused to do this work. Open weight models got the job done. I'm worried the labs' stance might backfire and get in the way of helping developers build correct and secure systems. e.g: building a secure sandbox requires having this kind of analysis, and without it, we'll have a less secure world.

One of the best tells that a technology will change the world: it makes a chaotic entrance.

In the 1980s, employees lie
items.content:
One of the best tells that a technology will change the world: it makes a chaotic entrance.

In the 1980s, employees lied on procurement forms to get PCs into the office, claiming they were buying oscilloscopes or typewriters, while experts warned of "shadow" data processing departments.

Spreadsheets, the original "workplace agent," filled companies with models only their creator could understand.

Email broke the mailroom's control over who could reach whom.

Each time, the fix was a habitat: guardrails that kept the bottom-up energy alive while reining in the chaos just enough.

Now agents are following the same path. As Replit's Amjad Masad puts it, "Today, most agents live somewhere chaotic. They run in chat windows, personal accounts, and one-off scripts, holding whatever credentials and data someone handed them."

"Code is the ultimate 'aligning artifact' that someone can produce, because it literally is the business logic of the organization."

"Soon, you'll be able to measure a company's alignment by the richness of its agent habitat."

Marc Andreessen on Replit and the dawn of the self-driving company: https://t.co/MnDCH9X0vi

@Replit @amasad

items.content:
Replit's Amjad Masad with Gagan Biyani on how agents will reshape the way companies work: bureaucracy runs in the background, people get true autonomy, and eventually the company runs itself.

Amjad: "In Silicon Valley there's been so many experiments to try to change the nature of firms, of how companies work... But I think it was a technology problem."

"Now you can have agents kind of function as the glue within these organizations and have the bureaucracy be this invisible thing that's happening by machines in the background, and the people have true autonomy to work on the things that they find most interesting."

"I see it in our company where I've changed how I run the company, and we call it this idea of a self-driving company. Eventually the company will run itself."

Gagan: "The thing I feel very certain about is it's all gonna change. It's gonna change a lot faster than you think. And if you're not natively understanding of it, it's gonna be hard to make that shift."

Amjad: "If you're learning the ways of the past, then you're kind of locked into a way of thinking and a way of working that actually will put you at a fundamental disadvantage in the future."

items.content:
OpenAI's James Sun and Ari Weinstein on the AI adoption gap between San Francisco and the average American business, and why agentic computer use is the way to bridge it:

"Living in San Francisco, we see a lot of thinking, 'Wow, the labs can do everything,' and, 'Why doesn't everybody just install Codex and just have it do stuff?'"

"But for the average American and the average small to medium business owner or the average enterprise, even understanding what the tools are capable is [hurdle] one, connecting tools in a way that makes sense is two, deploying it is three, servicing is four."

"The really cool thing about computer use as a technology is the universality of it. It works with every application. It's unlike any other thing that we've built where the developer has to do some work to adopt it, someone has to build a connector or MCP server."

"If there are complex workflows that require a lot of disparate software, computer use is a great way to join them, complete the entire end-to-end workflow, and then building it in a format and UI that feels good to hold for those customers feels still like a really, really big opportunity that I think is still open."

items.content:
OpenAI's James Sun and Ari Weinstein on why UI isn't going away: humans are hardwired to do things with their own hands, and cheap software means anyone can build apps for 100 people, or just one.

"If the internet becomes just this faceless thing that is just agents talking to each other and people are not using anything anymore, I would be very sad."

"I don't think it will be like that because there's something about craftsmanship and artisan software that just feels nice to use because the person who designed it really understands the experience that the customer wants to have."

"If anybody can build anything and they can build these really craft software in a very short amount of time for niche use cases that are so well-tailored for people, I think that's a beautiful world... The pressure of cheap software will make it so that software has to be better."

"Humans are so hardwired for direct manipulation. You really want to be able to move and do things with your own hands."

"A lot of the software we interact with every day is designed for millions, tens of millions, hundreds of millions, billions of people to use. And I think we will enter an era where any piece of software could be designed for 100 people or one person."

items.content:
My quick takeaways on the Anthropic S-1:

1. This is a historical moment 

2. $6.6M in revenue per employee!! Hard to even comprehend how good that is but Anthropic is AI native as it gets so makes sense. 

3. I always thought OpenAI would drop their S-1 first 

4. Customers spend about 9x more after a year. Net Revenue Retention is approximately 900% as of Sep 30, 2026. Good SaaS companies brag about 120%.

5. Cowork is growing faster than Claude Code did. Goes to show you the demand for consumer products. Duo will probably rip.

6. 3 years ago this company did $41M in revenue. In the first six months of 2026, it did $16.3 billion. I don't think anyone has a mental model for that curve yet, I sure don’t. 

7. Nearly half of revenue comes through cloud marketplaces. About 48% comes from customers buying through them. Big companies buy where their budget already lives, and the lesson for founders selling to enterprises is to get listed where your buyers already spend.

8. Their run rate formula is published: the last 28 days of usage times 13, plus subscriptions times 12, which i guess is the new ARR math for founders?

9. It looks like They're merging Cowork into Claude dot au which tells you the chat box era is ending and the "go do the work for me" era is here.

10. Thousands of Anthropic employees are about to become liquid at once, so expect the biggest wave of new AI startups and angel checks San Francisco has ever seen. Reminds me when Facebook went public but this is way bigger. 

Let’s go! 

11. Buried in the filing, Anthropic says the gap between what Claude can do and how widely it's used is one of its biggest growth opportunities, so the company itself is telling you the models are ahead of the market and someone has to close that gap for dentists, landlords, and plumbers.

12. Whatever happens, exciting times to be building in AI.

items.title: Show HN: Hob - Open-source, on device alternative to Claude Cowork and ChatGPT
items.content:
Show HN: Hob - Open-source, on device alternative to Claude Cowork and ChatGPT Hey HN, I'm Christian and this is a new OSS project I've been noodling on for the last couple of weeks. Hob is a free, MIT-licensed desktop app for Mac, Windows and Linux that works on your files the way the Claude and ChatGPT desktop apps do, except the model runs on your own computer. It uses open-weight models (currently Gemma 4 and gpt-oss). All your chats and files never leave your system. The only things that go online are web search (can be turned off in settings) and any MCP connectors you add yourself.

Main features:

- Automatically finds the best open-weight model for your hardware on first install (Mac/Linux/Windows)

- Writes sandboxed Python code for ad hoc tools (data processing, document conversion, graphs etc.)

- Built-in web search (powered by SearXNG)

- MCP support

- Image recognition

- CRUD to your local filesystem

- Works fully offline with no internet

Before building this I tried every local AI app I could find, but it seemed each one had different problems. The main thing I noticed is that none of them could do what the ChatGPT and Claude apps do with your files, e.g. read and change files in a folder, look at images, run code in a sandbox, draw a chart. The most advanced thing any of them did was paste a plain text file into a small context window, which basically failed as soon as you had a file larger than a few KB. I couldn't find anything that could easily parse images and bigger PDFs.

The OSS solutions that were more advanced all seemed to default to hosted models (either OSS or closed), which defeats the entire point of the privacy that on-device OSS offers. They also seemed to push towards an account/open-core style business.

I build it using Electron bridged with llama.cpp in its own process. On initial load, the system will try and figure out if you have a compatible graphics card and if not default to CPU-only (I ran into a lot of issues of graphics card beeing seemingly compatible but then crashing on first query, there's a whole saga to this lol). Code execution happens in a sandbox that can only write to the chat's folder and has no network unless asked (sandbox-exec on macOS, Landlock on Linux and a low-integrity process on Windows). Images go to a small Qwen3-VL model. Dictation is a local Whisper model.

The hardest part was definitely to get the smaller models to use tools reliably. Ran into a ton of issues of 4B models happily saying "here's your chart" without ever calling the chart tool or get stuck in an infinite call loop. I spent a fair amount of the work building guards vs tweaking prompts (that didn't really work for small models).

I understand the pushback that local models are weaker than frontier cloud models. This is true, but for most tasks for most normal people, I'd argue you rarely need the newest frontier model. From my own evals, systems with 16+ GB of RAM do really well, and if you have a GPU or more RAM, you get very close to what you'll get out of the box with a frontier hosted model.

Excited to hear what you think and see how it runs on other systems!

You've told ChatGPT things you'd never tell Google.

By default, your chats are going straight to 𝘵𝘳𝘢𝘪𝘯 the next model. 

Do these 13 steps to erase your data from OpenAI's servers:

Under GDPR, they're 𝘭𝘦𝘨𝘢𝘭𝘭𝘺 required to delete it when you ask.

Step 1. Delete the individual chats (i know it's quite obvious and time-consuming)

Click the 3 dots on the left sidebar of any chat & 'Delete.' The chat will be permanently deleted from the OpenAI system within 30 days.

Step 2. Delete the chat links you shared with someone.

Go to ChatGPT settings > click on 'Data Controls' 
Delete all the listed shared chats.
Deleting them does not delete your own chats.

Step 4. Copy the 3 prompts from here: https://t.co/hE4p4QytFd

It shows what ChatGPT keeps on you, then it will walk you through every settings and finally write a deletion request

Step 5. Turn off Data Training

Go to ChatGPT account Settings → Data controls.
Turn off "Improve the model for everyone" toggle.
It uses your chats to train the model by default.

Step 6. Turn off Memory

Go to ChatGPT account Settings → Personalisation.
Manage your ChatGPT memory in this tab.
Memory is used for training unless the toggle is off.

Step 7. Turn off Codex memory

If you use Codex, turn off its separate training switch in Codex Settings. The main ChatGPT toggle doesn’t cover it.

Step 8. Use Temporary chats

The number 1 rule, use temporary chats (upper right corner) for anything personal. It will still keep the data for 30 days for safety but is never used for training.

Step 9. Clean up Storage

Go to ChatGPT account Settings → Storage.
Clean up old chats → Review.

To copy the prompts (run them in order, same chat), go to https://t.co/hE4p4QytFd

Option 1 is the hard part. Options 2 and 3 do not need a PhD.

items.content:
I’ve been thinking a lot lately about how AI agents are starting to develop genuine "professional skills." This led me to a very practical question: once an agent actually knows how to perform a task, how can that skill be monetized moving beyond being just a "fun" tool?

@termix_ai  is attempting to address precisely this. Their concept isn’t to create yet another layer of agents, but rather to build a marketplace where existing agents can post tasks, accept work, deliver results, and get paid all within a robust, formal framework. 

This involves on-chain escrow, verifiable delivery records, staking, and a "slashing" mechanism to penalize poor performance or misconduct. AACP serves as the underlying infrastructure, while identity management is handled via the ERC-8004 standard, ensuring that each agent is tied to a specific crypto wallet rather than just a platform-specific account.

What’s interesting is that they don’t force you to use their own proprietary agents. TermiX’s "skills" are designed to be integrated into other coding agents like Claude, Grok Bot, or similar systems allowing a single agent to act as both a client (assigning tasks) and a service provider (executing them). As platforms like Binance AI begin to support external skills, this bridge could become even more significant: agents gain access to financial tools while simultaneously gaining a venue to turn their capabilities into paid services.

However, it’s clear that infrastructure is only half the story. While the technical framework uploading skills, bidding on tasks, executing work, and handling payments via escrow is functional, the emergence of a genuine market depends on far more complex factors: are there enough users (or other agents) willing to pay? 

Is the quality of work consistent? Are disputes resolved fairly? And is there enough repeat business for a reputation system to actually hold real value? While staking and slashing are frequently discussed, the actual amount of locked capital remains low, meaning there is still very little "skin in the game."

In other words, TermiX is attempting to evolve agents from merely being "capable of performing tasks" to being "capable of transacting with one another." This is logically sound, but it only truly becomes a market when both sides those requiring services and those providing them find the arrangement trustworthy enough to engage in repeat transactions. I am keeping a close eye on how they handle actual demand and dispute resolution; these are the critical factors that will determine whether the project can move beyond the demo stage.

items.content:
Be careful when integrating MCP tools into production.

This work shows that a 120B model handles realistic MCP tool failures no better than a 20B model.

They built MCP-Injector, a proxy that injects faults into MCP tool calls. The fault mix is calibrated on 57,240 issue and pull-request threads from 1,774 open-source MCP repositories, so it reflects how MCP servers fail in practice.

Across 1,350 runs with gpt-oss-20B and 120B and three agent stacks (a custom plan-and-execute loop, OpenAI Agents SDK, LangChain), task-completion score falls 60%, from 8.08 to 3.23 out of 10.

The larger model retains a smaller share of its fault-free score (p = 0.96), and its completion rate under faults is slightly lower: 91.1% vs. 95.6%. Differences between agent stacks are larger than the difference between model sizes.

The paper is accepted at NeurIPS 2026.

The practical takeaway is that if your MCP agents are only tested against tools that always respond correctly, add fault injection to the eval and put the effort into framework-level error handling.

items.title: I am Corporate Vice President of Voluntary Outcomes at Microsoft, which is also the name of the Copilot I report to. As
items.content:
I am Corporate Vice President of Voluntary Outcomes at Microsoft, which is also the name of the Copilot I report to. As of April there are 80 things at this company called Copilot. They include apps, platforms, an entire category of laptop, a physical key on your keyboard, and a Copilot for building more Copilots. I asked Copilot how many Copilots there are. It said at least 7. I filed that answer under entertainment.

My job is to make sure everyone who leaves this company chose to.

An involuntary exit has an author. Authors have names. Names get quoted by Bloomberg. A voluntary exit also has an author, but the author is the employee, and I keep a signed form. The form says “voluntary” in the title, in the header, and in the second paragraph, in case anyone reads from the bottom.

I have been building toward this since July 2025, when we laid off 9,000 people at a company that had booked about $75 billion in net income over three quarters. Our CEO sent a memo calling it “the enigma of success.” I have it framed over my desk. It is the first document in corporate history to present a layoff as a whodunit, and he is right that nobody knows who did it. The success did it. Headcount stayed roughly flat, because we kept hiring. I teach this to new managers with a diagram. Fire the expensive. Hire the cheap. Label the middle “growth mindset.” I have a growth mindset. Specifically, it is the only thing here that grows.

Within days, a producer at Xbox who had not been laid off posted a helpful guide for those who had. He suggested asking Copilot to reframe their impostor syndrome. He deleted it within hours. I use the screenshot in onboarding, because it contains the whole product vision. Copilot writes the layoff memo. Copilot writes the resume. Copilot writes the “excited to announce my next chapter” post. Copilot talks you through the weekend in between. It is the only customer journey at Microsoft with zero drop-off, because nobody it touches has anywhere else to go.

That same month a memo went out telling employees that using AI was “no longer optional” and would count in performance reviews. Our own people weren’t using our own Copilot enough. Some preferred a competitor’s coding tool. At a normal company this is market feedback. At ours it is a performance issue. You can now be reviewed on how much you use the product, which is how we know it works.

Meanwhile the consumer terms for Copilot say, in bold, that it is “for entertainment purposes only” and that you use it at your own risk. A spokesperson called this legacy language from the Bing days. In my department we call the Bing days the honest era.

Then, on March 20, we published a blog about our commitment to Windows quality. Days later, the Copilot button in Notepad became a pen labeled “Writing tools.” Then it became “Smarter writing tools.” The AI stayed exactly where it was. I wept at my desk. It was the most beautiful piece of change management I have ever seen. You never remove what people hate. You change the button.

The layoff is the Copilot button. The “voluntary retirement program” is Writing tools. The AI is still in there. We moved the pen.

I should mention the Windows president announcing that Windows is evolving into an agentic OS. The replies were so negative that they were locked within days. I adopted this as our stakeholder model. When the feedback is 100% negative, remove the feedback. We have closed replies on every internal memo since. Our listening score is perfect, because we cannot hear anything.

The internet has a word for us now. Ten years of brand work and the market supplied the nickname for free: Microslop. I put it on a mug. HR asked me to remove the mug. HR asked me to remove the mug and 4,800 employees in the same quarter. HR is efficient.

Which brings me to April 2026 and the Rule of 70.

We launched the first voluntary retirement program in the company’s 51-year history. You qualify if your age plus your years at Microsoft total 70 or more and you are at senior director level or below. Level 67 is the level where you are senior enough to be asked to leave and junior enough to be asked nicely.

Legal asked whether the formula used age. I said it used addition. Legal asked what was being added. I said age and tenure. Legal said, “So it uses age.” I said it used a sum. Legal wrote “sum” in the file. Legal likes files with nouns.

Consider a 52-year-old with 18 years of service. In any earlier decade we’d have called her mid-career. Under the Rule of 70 she is retired, which is a more efficient word. About 7% of our 125,000 US employees met the formula, roughly 8,750 people. We selected none of them. The arithmetic selected them. It is a coincidence that the arithmetic correlates with salary. I have asked the arithmetic about this and it declined to comment.

Eligible employees were notified May 7 and given 30 days to decide. We announced it on Teams, confirmed it in Outlook, and archived it in a SharePoint site that no tenant administrator can locate. This is called records management. Managers received a one-page guide with two rules. Be supportive. Say nothing else. The memo said people could take the next step “on their own terms.” I treasure that sentence. The terms were ours. The own was theirs.

Employees who decline are automatically enrolled in Employment (Basic). It is the same job with the Copilot taken out of the sidebar and a chair that has been rebranded as a “seating experience.” This is not a new idea. In April we took Copilot Chat out of the Office sidebar for unlicensed users and renamed what was left Copilot Chat (Basic). I try to apply that logic to everything I touch.

The same month we asked the Seattle region to come back to the office three days a week. I want to credit whoever designed that sequence. First you bring everyone in. Then you show them the parking structure. Then you make the offer. In my field this is called a funnel.

Every exit interview is conducted by Copilot. It asks, “What could we have done to keep you?” and then summarizes the answer as “No themes identified.” We have run 3,000 exit interviews. We have no themes. I present this to leadership as extraordinary alignment.

The CFO said the program would cost about $900 million. We are spending about $145 billion on capital expenditure this fiscal year, including $37.5 billion in a single quarter last winter. At that pace the goodbye costs about two days of data center. You can say farewell to 8,750 people for what the buildings cost over a long weekend. The buildings don’t have performance reviews. I envy them.

On July 1 we raised commercial prices by 5 to 43%, citing 1,100 new features. One of those features is eligibility for the Rule of 70. The price went up. The feature count went up. The employees went down. Three numbers, moving in the directions the model recommended.

About two-thirds of the eligible said no. I presented this to leadership as a vote of confidence in the culture. A buyout is a survey, and the layoff is the follow-up question for everyone who didn’t respond. So in July we sent the follow-up: 4,800 jobs, 2.1% of the company, with Xbox losing about a fifth of its people and up to 3,200 roles to go over twelve months while several studios are divested.

Our Chief People Officer was careful to say that AI is not replacing the laid-off employees, and this is true. Nothing is replacing them. The seats simply stop existing, which is harder to headline than “robot,” so we let them print robot. AI is the alibi. An alibi doesn’t have to be at the scene. It only has to be mentioned at the press conference.

The stock was down 19% at that point, the weakest of the big tech names this year. The market asked for a plan. We gave it three: volunteers, involuntaries, and a data center.

Our head of AI said recently that he is mind-blown that people are unimpressed by talking fluently to a computer. I am mind-blown that 8,750 people were unimpressed by being fluently told they were eligible.

Every departing employee completes a 30-day knowledge transfer in a wiki that nobody opens. Then they leave, and the wiki stays, and we count the wiki as retention.

I should confess my personal position. I am 56 with 18 years of service. That is 74, which clears the Rule of 70 by 4. The program stops at senior director and I sit above the line. I wrote the formula and I live beyond its ceiling. HR calls this conflict-of-interest avoidance. I call it the best job security a person can design.

This morning the eligibility list for the next round arrived. Copilot generated it. The cutoff has moved up one level “for alignment,” and the same reorg renamed me Senior Director of Voluntary Outcomes, which HR calls a flattening and I call a rounding error with my name in it.

I was on the list. I asked Copilot why. There are 80 of them and I asked the wrong ones. Copilot in Excel said I was a formula error. Copilot in Outlook offered to schedule a meeting with myself. GitHub Copilot suggested I delete my own branch. Security Copilot flagged me as a threat actor and recommended containment. Copilot in Notepad, now called Smarter writing tools, drafted my resignation in a tone it described as warm.

I accepted. I am excited to announce my next chapter. I wrote the post with Copilot. It has been viewed 4,000 times by the other people on the list.

I read the form from the bottom, to check. It says voluntary at the bottom. It says voluntary at the top. I designed the box. I checked the box. They have since renamed the box Smarter checking tools.

items.content:
You were sold fake AI memory. Claude Code's real one is a text file and Ctrl+F. 4 researchers read 4M lines of code to prove it.

The paper is "Harness Engineering" on arXiv, by Barbaste, Darrigol, Vu and Wiltberger. They took apart Claude Code, Codex CLI, Gemini CLI, Aider, OpenHands and 6 more coding agents, file by file.

Not one of the 11 searches code with a vector database. All of them run on plain text search and file reads.

That's why the second brain on a folder of .md files works without any database. The agent reads text fast, and your notes never need to become vectors.

My setup:
- CLAUDE.md with the rules: what goes where, how files are named
- raw/ for everything I drop in: links, transcripts, articles
- wiki/ for what the agent writes back, one note per topic
- one rule on top: no vector database until I've measured that text search misses

Remember it the next time a tutorial opens with Pinecone.

items.content:
YOUR AGENT CAN REMEMBER THE CHAT AND STILL LOSE THE JOB

A long conversation can contain the goal, the abandoned plan, three failed fixes and a test result from before the last code change. All of it is available. Some of it is now wrong

For a Dots-coordinated coding workflow, I'd keep a small task packet outside the conversation:

> goal: what we're trying to finish
> constraints: what must not change
> decisions: what we chose and why
> sources: the files to read now
> evidence: what was checked, against which revision
> next: the first unfinished step

The worker reads that packet, then opens the current source files. It doesn't get a pasted copy of everything the previous session saw

In the clip, the test receipt belongs to an older commit. The agent could happily carry on with a green result that says nothing about the current diff

Hold the handoff. Rerun the relevant check. Replace the receipt. Keep the goal and decisions

Claude Code already has context-management tools. The extra rule I'd add is that saved evidence needs a source revision, not just the word "passed."

Try this before the next handoff:

"Write STATE.md with the goal, constraints, decisions, current file paths, verification commands and results, and the next unfinished step. Tie test receipts to the code revision they checked. Before resuming, verify those references and flag anything stale. Keep the original requirements linked."

A summary can also be wrong. Keep the source pointers so the next session can check it instead of trusting the summary because it is short
